limitations: The forecast is a single deterministic remaining-hours model with fixed rates and nonlabor commitments; it does not provide probabilistic ranges, productivity changes, escalation, or contingency-balance treatment.
The cost variance metric compares total actual cost to total baseline budget, so it is a remaining-budget indicator rather than a classic earned-value cost variance to date.

The data are notably rounded and tidy: WP1 and WP2 exactly consume baseline effort, and completed effort values are round numbers. This reduces occupational realism even though the calculations remain coherent.

The baseline lacks a cost-category breakdown, explicit dependency network, and stated contingency balance, which limits precision in downstream date-change approval analysis and contingency recommendations.

The project brief says approximately the first third of baseline effort has been consumed, while supplied effort totals imply 1,700 of 4,000 hours completed (42.5%) and 1,936 planned (48.4%); this is loose but not fatal.
